tasks.title: Quasipolynomial corners bounds
tasks.summary: Prove the stated quantitative bound for subsets of a finite abelian group squared that contain no nontrivial corner.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from additive combinatorics. A *corner* in `G × G`
(for a finite abelian group `G`) is a triple `(x, y), (x + d, y),
(x, y + d)` with `d ≠ 0`. The theorem states: there is a constant
`c > 0` such that for every finite abelian group `G`, every corner-free
`A ⊆ G × G` satisfies `|A| ≤ |G|²·exp(−c·(log|G|)^{1/600})`.
tasks.reference: Michael Jaber, Yang P. Liu, Shachar Lovett, Anthony Ostuni, Mehtaab Sawhney. Quasipolynomial Bounds for the Corners Theorem. FOCS, 2025.
tasks.note: The full parameter conditions and quantitative bound are fixed by the task statement.

tasks.title: Universal optimality of Dijkstra's algorithm
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from algorithm analysis. A distance order of a directed graph with a source s is a total order of the vertices in which every vertex other than s has an incoming forward arc (an arc from an earlier vertex); write D for the number of distance orders and F for the maximum number of forward arcs of any distance order.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from algorithm analysis. A *distance order* of a
directed graph with a source `s` is a total order of the vertices in
which every vertex other than `s` has an incoming *forward arc* (an arc
from an earlier vertex); write `D` for the number of distance orders and
`F` for the maximum number of forward arcs of any distance order. The
theorem states: there is a constant `C > 0` such that on every directed
graph with `n > 2` vertices (all reachable from the source), Dijkstra
traces exist on every non-negative arc-length assignment; every Dijkstra
trace has time at most `C·(m + log₂ D)` and at most `C·(F + log₂ D)`
comparisons, where the costs are those of a heap with the working-set
bound; every correct time-model algorithm (decision trees with
incidence-list access) spends at least `(m + log₂ D)/C` time on some arc
lengths and representation; and every correct comparison-model algorithm
(linear-function decision trees) makes at least
`(F − n + 1 + log₂ D)/C` comparisons on some arc lengths. In other
words, Dijkstra's algorithm with a working-set-bound heap is universally
optimal in time, and universally optimal in comparisons up to an
additive term in `n`. An interval-DAG bound is given as the hypothesis
`hidag`.
tasks.reference: Bernhard Haeupler, Richard Hladík, Václav Rozhoň, Robert E. Tarjan, Jakub Tětek. Universal Optimality of Dijkstra via Beyond-Worst-Case Heaps. FOCS, 2024.

tasks.title: O(sqrt k) discrepancy for column-sparse matrices at large k
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from discrepancy theory. Given a matrix A ∈ {0,±1}^{m×n} where every column has at most k non-zero entries, the discrepancy is the minimum over ±1 colorings x of ‖Ax‖∞ — how evenly the columns can be split into two parts.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from discrepancy theory. Given a matrix
`A ∈ {0,±1}^{m×n}` where every column has at most `k` non-zero entries,
the discrepancy is the minimum over ±1 colorings `x` of `‖Ax‖∞` — how
evenly the columns can be split into two parts. It is conjectured that `disc(A) = O(√k)`
for every `k`. The theorem
(`sparse_column_discrepancy_large_k`) states: there are constants `c, C > 0` such that
every `{0,±1}` matrix `A` with at most `k` non-zero entries per column
and `k ≥ c (log n)²` has a ±1 coloring with `‖Ax‖∞ ≤ C √k` (for
`2 ≤ n`).
tasks.reference: Nikhil Bansal, Haotian Jiang. Decoupling via Affine Spectral-Independence: Beck-Fiala and Komlós Bounds Beyond Banaszczyk. STOC, 2026.

tasks.title: Discrete bidding games
tasks.summary: Prove that a player meeting the budget threshold has a legal strategy that keeps energy nonnegative in an integer-weighted directed graph.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from the theory of discrete-bidding games. An energy
discrete-bidding game is played on a finite directed graph with integer
edge weights and total budget `k`: each turn both players bid, the higher
bidder moves the token and pays the opponent; Pres wins iff the energy
stays non-negative forever. The theorem states: there exists a legal,
budget-agnostic Pres strategy that `M`-wins from every configuration
`⟨v, B⟩` with `B ≥ Th(v)`, where `Th(v)` is the threshold budget (the
minimal budget with finite energy threshold) and
`M = (k + 1)·(W + max_v Energy(v, Th(v)))` is explicit. The determinacy of
reachability discrete-bidding games is given as the hypothesis `hdet`.
tasks.reference: Guy Avni, Suman Sadhukhan. Mean-Payoff and Energy Discrete-Bidding Games. CSL, 2026.
tasks.note: Determinacy of the associated reachability bidding game is a supplied assumption.

tasks.title: Folded Reed–Solomon list decoding
tasks.summary: Prove the prescribed list-decoding bound: every Hamming ball at the stated radius contains at most the allowed number of codewords.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from coding theory. A folded Reed–Solomon code packs
the evaluations of a low-degree polynomial `f` at consecutive powers of
a multiplicative generator `γ` into blocks: the `i`-th symbol of the
encoding is the block `f(αᵢ), f(γαᵢ), …, f(γ^{s−1}αᵢ)`. A code is
*list-decodable* with radius `ρ` and list size `L` if no Hamming ball
of radius `ρ` contains more than `L` codewords. The theorem states:

> For `ε > 0`, `1 ≤ k < N`, `s ∣ N`, `n = N / s`, `q > n`, rate
> `R = k/N`, and any `L > (1−R−ε)/ε` and
> `s > L·(L−1)·R/(εL−(1−R−ε)) + L − 1`, the folded Reed–Solomon code
> `FRS^{(s,γ)}_{n,k}(α)` at appropriate evaluation points is
> `(1 − R − ε, L)` list-decodable.
tasks.reference: Yeyuan Chen, Zihan Zhang. Explicit Folded Reed-Solomon and Multiplicity Codes Achieve Relaxed Generalized Singleton Bounds. STOC, 2025.
tasks.note: The target is the folded Reed–Solomon theorem; the task fixes all parameter assumptions.

tasks.title: Optimal proximity gaps for algebraic codes
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from coding theory. A code has a proximity gap if, along a low-degree parametric curve of words, either almost no curve points are close to the code or all of them are; the formal statement is about mutual correlated agreement (MCA) for subspace-design codes (codes whose low-dimensional subspaces lose dimension quickly when pinned at coordinates).
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from coding theory. A code has a *proximity gap* if,
along a low-degree parametric curve of words, either almost no curve
points are close to the code or all of them are; the formal statement is
about *mutual correlated agreement* (MCA) for *subspace-design* codes
(codes whose low-dimensional subspaces lose dimension quickly when
pinned at coordinates). The theorem states:

> Every `τ`-subspace-design code has mutual correlated agreement with
> proximity `1 − τ((ℓ+1)t) − 3/(2t)`, error
> `t·ℓ·(ℓ+1)·(m(1−τ((ℓ+1)t)) + 2t²)/|F|`, and slack `1/m`
> (for `2 ≤ m ≤ 4t`, under the stated field-size and boundary
> hypotheses).

Two ingredients are given as hypotheses: a pruning guarantee
(`PruningGuarantee`) and a list-size bound (`ListSizeBound`), both
packaged as hypothesis-level definitions in the file.
tasks.reference: Rohan Goyal, Venkatesan Guruswami. Optimal Proximity Gaps for Subspace-Design Codes and (Random) Reed-Solomon Codes. STOC, 2026.

tasks.title: Exponential lower bound for linear 3-query locally correctable codes
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from coding theory. A linear 3-query locally correctable code in normal form is a systematic linear code ℒ : F₂ᵏ → F₂ⁿ together with, for every coordinate u, a 3-uniform hypergraph matching H u of d0 edges such that x_u = Σ_{v ∈ C} x_v (over F₂) for every edge C ∈ H u and every codeword x.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from coding theory. A *linear 3-query locally
correctable code* in *normal form* is a systematic linear code
`ℒ : F₂ᵏ → F₂ⁿ` together with, for every coordinate `u`, a 3-uniform
hypergraph matching `H u` of `d0` edges such that `x_u = Σ_{v ∈ C} x_v`
(over F₂) for every edge `C ∈ H u` and every codeword `x`. The theorem
states: there is an absolute constant `C > 0` such that every such code
with `d0 ≥ δn` satisfies `k ≤ C·(log₂ n)⁸/δ²`, i.e.
`n ≥ 2^{(δ²k/C)^{1/8}}`. A linear 2-LDC lower bound is given as a
hypothesis.
tasks.reference: Pravesh K. Kothari, Peter Manohar. An Exponential Lower Bound for Linear 3-Query Locally Correctable Codes. STOC, 2024.

tasks.title: Query lower bound for monotonicity testing of Boolean functions
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from property testing. A Boolean function f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1} is monotone if flipping a coordinate of an input from 0 to 1 can never flip the value from 1 to 0, and it is ε-far from monotone if every monotone function disagrees with it on at least an ε fraction of the cube.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from property testing. A Boolean function
`f : {0,1}ⁿ → {0,1}` is *monotone* if flipping a coordinate of an input
from 0 to 1 can never flip the value from 1 to 0, and it is `ε`-far from
monotone if every monotone function disagrees with it on at least an `ε`
fraction of the cube. A monotonicity tester queries values of an unknown
`f` and must tell the two cases apart; the question is how many queries an
adaptive algorithm needs. The theorem states: for every integer constant
`ℓ ≥ 1` there are a testing distance `ε > 0` and an error `δ > 0` such that
for all sufficiently large `m` (with `n = m²`) no randomized adaptive
algorithm whose deterministic members all have depth at most
`q = n^{1/2−1/(4ℓ+2)}/log₂ n` can both accept the yes distribution `Dyes`
with probability at least `1 − δ` and, jointly under the no distribution
`Dno`, accept an `ε`-far-from-monotone function with probability at most
`δ`. The two distributions and the stronger oracle they are queried through
are defined in the file.
tasks.reference: Mark Chen, Xi Chen, Hao Cui, William Pires, Jonah Stockwell. Boolean Function Monotonicity Testing Requires (Almost) n^{1/2} Queries. STOC, 2026.

tasks.title: Log-squared randomized lower bound for small-set chasing
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from the theory of online algorithms. In small-set chasing on a finite metric space, an online algorithm controls one server; each request is a finite subset S of points, and serving it means moving into S, paying the distance travelled.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from the theory of online algorithms. In *small-set
chasing* on a finite metric space, an online algorithm controls one
server; each request is a finite subset `S` of points, and serving it
means moving into `S`, paying the distance travelled. The theorem
states:

> There are a universal constant `c > 0` and a threshold `n₀` such that
> for every `n ≥ n₀` there is an `n`-point metric space `M` and a start
> point for which small-set chasing admits a distributional lower bound
> of `c·(log₂ n / log₂ log₂ n)²`: a finite sample space carrying a
> distribution of request sequences with positive expected optimal cost
> such that every deterministic online algorithm pays, in expectation,
> at least `c·(log₂ n / log₂ log₂ n)²` times the expected optimal cost.
tasks.reference: Sébastien Bubeck, Christian Coester, Yuval Rabani. The Randomized k-Server Conjecture is False!. STOC, 2023.

tasks.title: Multiflow-multicut gap lower bound on planar graphs
tasks.summary: The theorem is a pure-graph statement behind a multiflow–multicut gap lower bound. A small-diameter decomposition distribution SDD(G, 2w, p) of a graph is a probability distribution on edge sets whose removal leaves components of diameter < 2w, under which every edge is cut with probability at most p.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem is a graph statement underlying a lower bound on the multiflow–multicut ratio. A small-diameter decomposition distribution `SDD(G, 2w, p)` randomly chooses edges to remove. Any two vertices left in the same connected component must have distance `< 2w` in the original graph `G`, before those edges were removed. Each edge is removed with probability at most `p`.

A cactus is a graph in which every edge belongs to at most one cycle. The theorem states: for even `w ≥ 2` and `0 < p < 1`, if every finite cactus graph admits an `SDD(G, 2w, p)` distribution, then `8/7 ≤ w·p`.

Through the equivalence between these decompositions and multiflow–multicut ratios, this yields a lower bound of `16/7` for cactus graphs and hence for planar graphs. That equivalence is background context; the formal task proves the graph-decomposition statement.
tasks.reference: Sina Kalantarzadeh, Nikhil Kumar. Improved Lower Bounds on Multiflow-Multicut Gaps. APPROX, 2025.

tasks.title: Subtraction in arithmetic formulas
tasks.summary: Prove that certain graph polynomials admit small arithmetic formulas using subtraction while every monotone arithmetic formula requires exponential size.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from arithmetic complexity. An arithmetic formula
computes a multivariate polynomial using `+`, `−`, `×` gates; it is
*monotone* if it has no subtraction gate and all its constants are
non-negative. From any `n`-vertex graph `G` one builds the *graph
polynomial* `P_G = Σ_{a ∈ {0,1}ⁿ} (e(G[supp a]) − 1)² · ∏ᵢ x_{i,aᵢ}`
on the variable set `{x_{i,0}, x_{i,1}}` (all coefficients
non-negative). The theorem states: for every degree `d ≥ 2` there are
a constant `c > 0` and a threshold `N₀` such that for all `n ≥ N₀` and
every `n`-vertex `d`-regular spectral expander `G` (second largest
eigenvalue in absolute value of the adjacency matrix at most `d^{3/4}`),
the graph polynomial `P_G` is computed by an explicit arithmetic
formula of size at most `35·(e(G)+1)²·n`, but every monotone arithmetic
formula computing `P_G` has size at least `2^{c·n}`. A random-matching
existence lemma is given as the hypothesis `expanderMatchingProp`
(with per-degree constants).
tasks.reference: Bruno Cavalar, Théo Borém Fabris, Partha Mukhopadhyay, Srikanth Srinivasan, Amir Yehudayoff. Negations Are Powerful Even in Small Depth. STOC, 2026.
tasks.note: The task supplies a random-matching assumption. This concerns arithmetic formulas and monotonicity.

tasks.title: Near-optimal alphabet-soundness tradeoff for two-query PCP
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from PCP combinatorics. An inner PCP encodes a linear function f : F_q^n → F_q by its restrictions to subspaces, and the soundness analysis works with zoom-out function pairs (W, g): a subspace W and a linear g : W → F_q agreeing with the encoding table on a noticeable fraction of the 2ℓ-dimensional subspaces L with Q ⊆ L ⊆ W.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from PCP combinatorics. An inner PCP encodes a linear
function `f : F_q^n → F_q` by its restrictions to subspaces, and the
soundness analysis works with *zoom-out function pairs* `(W, g)`: a
subspace `W` and a linear `g : W → F_q` agreeing with the encoding table
on a noticeable fraction of the `2ℓ`-dimensional subspaces `L` with
`Q ⊆ L ⊆ W`. A pair is `(C, ζ)`-*maximal* if no proper extension reaches
agreement `ζ·C`. The theorem states: under two packaged hypotheses (a
many-zoomouts refinement and a generic-family sampling bound), for every
`δ > 0` there is `ℓ₀` such that for all `ℓ ≥ ℓ₀` and all ambient
dimensions `n ≥ 2^{100}·q^ℓ`, for every table `T` on `F_q^n`, every
subspace `Q` of dimension `r₁ ≤ 10/δ`, and every `C ≥ q^{-2(1-δ³)ℓ}`, the
number of `(C, 1/5)`-maximal zoom-out function pairs with respect to `T`
on `Q` of ambient codimension at most `10/δ` is at most
`(160/δ)·C^{-2}·q^{100(t-1)!(10/δ)²ℓ/ξ}` (with `ξ = δ⁵` and
`t = ⌈2^{2+10/δ₂}⌉!`, `δ₂ = ξ/100`).
tasks.reference: Dor Minzer, Kai Zhe Zheng. Near Optimal Alphabet-Soundness Tradeoff PCPs. STOC, 2024.

tasks.title: Linear kernel for independent-set reconfiguration in planar graphs
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from graph reconfiguration. An independent set in a graph is a set of vertices no two of which are adjacent; picture a token on each of its vertices.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from graph reconfiguration. An independent set in a
graph is a set of vertices no two of which are adjacent; picture a token
on each of its vertices. In the *token jumping* (TJ) model, one step
removes a single token from its vertex and places it on any other
vertex, provided the result is again an independent set. The ISR-TJ
problem asks, given a graph `G` and two size-`k` independent sets `Is`,
`It`, whether a sequence of such jumps transforms `Is` into `It`. A
*kernel* is a compression of the instance to an equivalent one whose
size is bounded by a function of `k` alone. Write `X := Is ∪ It` for the
*key vertices*; the vertices outside `X` are grouped into *projection
classes* by their neighborhood inside `X`, and `N2`/`N3` count the
nonempty classes on exactly 2, respectively at least 3, key vertices.
The theorem states:

> Fix `1 ≤ r` and `1 ≤ k`. Let `G` be a finite simple graph with no
> `K_{3,r}` minor, given together with a proper coloring with
> `max{r,6300} + 3` colors and with the bound
> `N2(G) + N3(G) ≤ 2^{5r+13}·(r+3)^{2r+5}·k`. Let `Is`, `It` be
> independent sets of size `k`. Then there is a vertex set `W ⊇ X` with
> `|W| ≤ K(r)·k`, where
> `K(r) = 2 + q + (r−1)·B + q·(B·(4r−1)+1)` for `q = max{r,6300}+3` and
> `B = 2^{5r+13}·(r+3)^{2r+5}`, such that `Is` reconfigures into `It`
> under token jumping if and only if it does so using only vertices of
> `W`.
tasks.reference: Nicolas Bousquet, Daniel W. Cranston. A Linear Kernel for Independent Set Reconfiguration in Planar Graphs. STACS, 2026.

tasks.title: Log-competitive memoryless algorithm for chasing positive bodies
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from online algorithms. In positive body chasing, an online algorithm sees a sequence of constraints in the nonnegative orthant and must maintain a feasible point while paying the weighted ℓ1 distance it moves.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from online algorithms. In *positive body chasing*, an
online algorithm sees a sequence of constraints in the nonnegative
orthant and must maintain a feasible point while paying for weighted increases in its coordinates. Each constraint is a single halfspace — a covering
constraint `⟨c^t, x⟩ ≥ 1` or a packing constraint `⟨p^t, x⟩ ≤ 1 + ε` —
and cost is measured by the *upward recourse*
`∑_t ∑_i w_i·(x^t_i − x^{t-1}_i)⁺`. The algorithm answers each violated
constraint with a single Kullback–Leibler divergence projection (a covering update
with an additive offset `ε/(4·d^t·c^t_i)`, where `d^t` is the row
sparsity); it is presented here only through a response bundle
`ChaseRun` of the properties the analysis uses (the trajectory and the
Karush–Kuhn–Tucker multipliers, with tightness and multiplier conditions, monotonicity,
and frozenness outside the support). The theorem states: the algorithm's
upward recourse is at most `K = (2 + ε)(1 + ε)·log(1 + 40d²/ε²)/ε`
times the upward recourse of every exactly-feasible benchmark
trajectory.
tasks.reference: Sayan Bhattacharya, Niv Buchbinder, Roie Levin, Thatchaphol Saranurak. Chasing Positive Bodies. FOCS, 2023.

tasks.title: Quantum versus classical witnesses
tasks.summary: Prove a conditional query and witness-size separation for spectral Forrelation: constant-query verification with n-qubit quantum witnesses versus polynomially bounded classical witnesses and queries.
tasks.question_markdown:
Spectral Forrelation is a decision problem about two subsets S and U of the Boolean hypercube. It asks whether a quantum state can be well supported on S in the standard basis and on U in the Fourier basis. The promise separates operator norm squared at least 59/100 from at most 57/100.

The formalized theorem compares query algorithms with different witnesses. For all sufficiently large n, an n-qubit quantum witness permits verification with a constant number of oracle queries. Every classical-witness algorithm whose witness length and query count are bounded by a·n^a misclassifies some promised instance. The theorem assumes witness-length-preserving amplification, core-matrix concentration and a compressed-oracle sampling bound.
tasks.reference: John Bostanci, Jonas Haferkamp, Chinmay Nirkhe, Mark Zhandry. Separating QMA from QCMA with a Classical Oracle. STOC, 2026.

tasks.title: Exponential worst-case lower bound for symmetric strategy improvement
tasks.summary: The theorem is about parity games. A parity game is played by two players on a finite directed graph: a pebble moves along edges, the owner of the current node chooses the move, and the winner is decided by the parity of the largest priority seen infinitely often.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem is about parity games. A parity game is played by two
players on a finite directed graph: a pebble moves along edges, the
owner of the current node chooses the move, and the winner is decided by
the parity of the largest priority seen infinitely often. *Strategy
improvement* evaluates a positional strategy by playing it against an
optimal counterstrategy and recording, for every start node, the *play
value* — the vector counting how often each priority occurs on the way
to the sink — and then switches to edges with a better valuation.
*Symmetric* strategy improvement (SSI) improves the strategies of both
players simultaneously, using each player's optimal counterstrategy to
select the other player's improving moves. The theorem states: an
explicit family of games `G_n` (with `2n+2` nodes) forces `2^{n+1} − 3`
iterations for **every** improvement rule — SSI needs exponentially many
iterations on `G_n` independently of the improvement rule. Formally: for
every `n ≥ 1` and every improvement rule `f`, no legal SSI iteration
chain on `G_n` starting from the initial strategy pair `(σ₀, τ₀)` whose
length is at most `2^{n+1} − 3` ends at a pair of optimal strategies.
tasks.reference: Tom van Dijk, Georg Loho, Matthew T. Maat. The Worst-Case Complexity of Symmetric Strategy Improvement. CSL, 2024.

tasks.title: Constant-competitive online 3-taxi on general metrics
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from online algorithms. In the (hard) k-taxi problem, k taxis move in a metric space and must serve online requests (r, s): some taxi must move to the pick-up point r (this empty movement is the only cost) and is then relocated to s for free.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from online algorithms. In the (hard) `k`-taxi
problem, `k` taxis move in a metric space and must serve online requests
`(r, s)`: some taxi must move to the pick-up point `r` (this empty
movement is the only cost) and is then relocated to `s` for free. The
theorem states: there is a constant `κ > 0` such that the algorithm
TripodTracker for `k = 3`, as given by the trajectory semantics of the
definition layer, has total online cost at most `κ` times the total
offline cost (no additive constant), for every initial state with
coinciding online/offline configurations and zero intervals and every
request sequence paired with offline choices.
tasks.reference: Christian Coester, Tze-Yang Poon. Online 3-Taxi on General Metrics. SODA, 2026.

tasks.title: Limits of one-query unitary synthesis
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from quantum query complexity. A one-query adversary is a triple (M, V, Pj): an isometry V : ℂ^N → ℂ^M and a projection Pj on ℂ^M.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from quantum query complexity. A one-query adversary
is a triple `(M, V, Pj)`: an isometry `V : ℂ^N → ℂ^M` and a projection
`Pj` on `ℂ^M`. It prepares a *binary phase state*
`|ψ_h⟩ = (1/√N) Σ_x h(x)|x⟩` for a Boolean function `h : [N] → {±1}`,
applies `V`, makes a single oracle query (the oracle `f : [M] → {±1}`
acts as the diagonal sign matrix `O_f`), and measures with `Pj`; its
acceptance probability is `p_A(h|f) = Re ⟨Vψ_h, O_f Pj O_f Vψ_h⟩`. For a
function family `R : [K] × [N] → {±1}`, the distinguishing advantage is
`Δ_A(R) = max_f [ E_k p_A(R_k|f) − E_h p_A(h|f) ]`. The theorem states:

> There is an absolute constant `C > 0` such that for every one-query
> adversary `(M, V, Pj)` with `1 ≤ M`, `1 ≤ K`, and all isometry
> weights positive, the expected distinguishing advantage over a
> uniformly random function family is at most `C·√(ln M / K)`.
tasks.reference: Alex Lombardi, Fermi Ma, John Wright. A One-Query Lower Bound for Unitary Synthesis and Breaking Quantum Cryptography. STOC, 2024.

tasks.title: Parallel repetition of three-player XOR games
tasks.summary: The theorem comes from game theory. A 3-XOR game G is given by a probability distribution μ over question triples (x, y, z) and a target t(x, y, z) in a finite abelian group A: the verifier samples (x, y, z) ~ μ, collects answers f(x), g(y), h(z) ∈ A from the three players, and accepts iff f(x) + g(y) + h(z) = t(x, y, z).
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from game theory. A *3-XOR game* `G` is given by a
probability distribution `μ` over question triples `(x, y, z)` and a
target `t(x, y, z)` in a finite abelian group `A`: the verifier samples
`(x, y, z) ~ μ`, collects answers `f(x), g(y), h(z) ∈ A` from the three
players, and accepts iff `f(x) + g(y) + h(z) = t(x, y, z)`. The *value*
`val(G)` is the best acceptance probability over all strategies. In the
*n-fold parallel repetition* the verifier samples `n` independent
challenges and the players must win all of them. An *embedding* of `μ`
into an abelian group is a triple of maps `σ, γ, ϕ` with
`σ(x) + γ(y) + ϕ(z) = 0` on the support of `μ`; `μ` *has no
`ℤ`-embeddings* if every embedding into `(ℤ, +)` is constant in each
coordinate. The theorem is stated conditionally on a packaged
additive-combinatorics input `FreimanAssumption` (part of the
definition layer), and states:

> If `val(G) < 1` and `μ` has no `ℤ`-embeddings, then
> `val(G^⊗n) ≤ 2^{−cn}` for some `c > 0` (depending on the game) and
> all `n ≥ 1`.
tasks.reference: Amey Bhangale, Mark Braverman, Subhash Khot, Yang P. Liu, Dor Minzer. Parallel Repetition for 3-Player XOR Games. STOC, 2025.

tasks.title: Pseudorandomness of Forrelation
tasks.summary: Prove pseudorandomness of the Forrelation distribution against the specified Boolean functions, with a bound controlled by second-order Fourier coefficients.
tasks.question_markdown:
The theorem comes from pseudorandomness. The *Forrelation distribution*
`F_n` is a distribution over pairs of Boolean functions
`f, g : {±1}ⁿ → {±1}`: first `f` is sampled uniformly at random, and
then, independently for each input `x`, the value `g(x)` is `±1` with
bias `trnc(√(ε2ⁿ)·f̂(x))`, where `ε = 1/(100n)`, `f̂` is the Fourier
coefficient of `f`, and `trnc` truncates to `[−1,1]`. A well-known
consequence of the theorem is pseudorandomness against
`AC⁰[2^poly(n), O(1)]` circuits; the statement packaged here is the more
general bound: for `N = 2ⁿ` and any Boolean `C` on `2N` variables all of
whose `±1`-restrictions have level-2 Fourier mass
`L_{1,2} = ∑_{|S|=2} |Ĉ(S)|` at most `t`,

|E_{(f,g)∼F_n}[C(tt f, tt g)] − E_{z uniform}[C(z)]| ≤ O(max(t,1)·log N/√N).

Two external facts are **packaged as hypotheses** (deep or textbook
results; your proof may assume them): a Gaussian-fooling theorem for
bounded level-2 Fourier mass (`gaussianFoolingProp`) and explicit Gaussian tail /
truncated-second-moment bounds (`gaussianTailProp`).

The single theorem you must prove:

`forrelation_pseudorandom` — there exists `K > 0` such that for every
`n ≥ 1`, every multilinear `C` on the `2N` variables that is `±1`-valued
on the cube, and every `t ≥ 0` bounding the level-2 Fourier mass of all
`±1`-restrictions of `C`, the displayed bound holds with constant `K`.
tasks.reference: Kretschmer, Qian, Sinha, Tal. Quantum cryptography in Algorithmica. STOC, 2023.
tasks.note: Two external Gaussian-distribution results are supplied as assumptions.

tasks.title: Hierarchical production planning
tasks.summary: This task is a deterministic single-player resource-compounding game. You own a small factory: N = 10 machine types, each existing at L = 4 levels.
tasks.question_markdown:
This is a deterministic single-player production game with `N = 10` machine types, each present at `L = 4` levels. The game lasts `T = 500` turns and starts with `K = 1` apple.

For each level and type, `B[level][id]` is the number of machines owned and starts at one. `P[level][id]` is the number of upgrades bought and starts at zero. The input supplies a production multiplier `A[id]` and a base upgrade cost `C[level][id]`.

Each turn has two phases:

1. **Action.** Buy at most one upgrade, or do nothing. An upgrade of type `id` at level `level` costs `C[level][id] * (P[level][id] + 1)` apples. It must be affordable at that moment; buying it deducts the cost and increments `P[level][id]` by one.
2. **Production.** Process levels in order from zero to three. At level zero, `apples += A[id] * B[0][id] * P[0][id]`. At each higher level `l`, `B[l-1][id] += B[l][id] * P[l][id]`. Machines produced during this phase start contributing from the following turn.

The raw score is

```
raw = round(100000 * log2(final_apples)).
```

Higher final apple counts are better. An unaffordable purchase or a nonpositive final apple count scores zero. The task’s scorer uses signed 64-bit arithmetic with wrap-around.
tasks.reference: AtCoder Heuristic Contest 058: Apple Incremental Game

tasks.title: One-dimensional bin packing
tasks.summary: Write a reusable solver that packs weighted items into equal-capacity bins while minimizing the number of bins.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **one-dimensional bin packing problem (BPP)**: you are given `n` items
with integer weights `w_1 .. w_n` and an unlimited supply of identical bins
of integer capacity `C`. Pack every item into bins so that no bin's total
weight exceeds `C`, using as few bins as possible. BPP is NP-hard — it is
NP-complete to decide whether two bins suffice.
tasks.reference: BPPLIB
tasks.note: The 39 final instances share one 1,170-second time pool. The pool must remain intact.

tasks.title: Cluster editing
tasks.summary: In the cluster editing problem you are given an undirected graph and may edit vertex pairs — add an edge where there is none, delete an edge where there is one.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **cluster editing** problem you are given an undirected graph and
may *edit* vertex pairs — add an edge where there is none, delete an edge
where there is one. The goal is to turn the graph into a **cluster
graph**: a disjoint union of cliques (every connected component is fully
connected inside). Each edited pair costs 1; the task is to minimize the
total number of edits. The problem is NP-hard and shows up wherever
objects must be partitioned into groups of mutual friends (computational
biology, deduplication, social network analysis).
tasks.reference: PACE 2021 (heuristic track)

tasks.title: Radio link frequency assignment (RLFAP)
tasks.summary: In the radio link frequency assignment problem, a set of radio links must each be assigned one transmit frequency.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **radio link frequency assignment problem**, a set of radio links
must each be assigned one transmit frequency. Every link has its own allowed
set of discrete frequencies, and interference between links is modelled by
two kinds of binary constraints on the assigned frequencies `f[x]`, `f[y]`:

- **hard equality constraints** `|f[x] − f[y]| = k` — must hold exactly
  (they typically pair a link with a frequency-shifted duplicate);
- **soft separation constraints** `|f[x] − f[y]| > k` — each violated one
  costs `costs[w]`, where `w` is the constraint's weight class; the
  objective is the total weighted violation, smaller is better.

This weighted partial constraint satisfaction problem is NP-hard.
tasks.reference: CALMA/CELAR benchmarks (ZIB archive; MiniZinc Challenge)

tasks.title: Christmas-tree forest partitioning
tasks.summary: You are given a planar graph: N = 1000 vertices, placed uniformly at random inside a circle, connected by the Delaunay triangulation of those points (1000 <= M <= 3000 edges).
tasks.question_markdown:
You are given a planar graph: `N = 1000` vertices, placed uniformly at
random inside a circle, connected by the **Delaunay triangulation** of
those points (`1000 <= M <= 3000` edges). Every vertex `v` has a positive
integer weight `A[v]` (between 1 and 100). The height limit is `H = 10`.

You must split the vertices into **rooted trees**: for every vertex you
either declare it a **root**, or choose one **parent**, such that

- the parent edge `(v, parent[v])` exists in the given graph,
- following parent pointers never loops (every chain ends at a root), so
  each vertex gets a well-defined **depth** `h[v]` (roots have `h = 0`),
- every depth is at most `H`: `h[v] <= 10`.

Each vertex may appear in exactly one tree, which the parent-pointer
structure guarantees automatically. Your raw score for an instance is

```
raw = 1 + sum_v (h[v] + 1) * A[v]
```
tasks.reference: AtCoder Heuristic Contest 041: Christmas Tree Cutting

tasks.title: Graph coloring
tasks.summary: In the graph coloring problem you are given an undirected graph and must assign a color to every vertex so that adjacent vertices get different colors, using as few colors as possible.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **graph coloring** problem you are given an undirected graph and
must assign a *color* to every vertex so that adjacent vertices get
different colors, using as few colors as possible. The smallest possible
number of colors is the chromatic number χ(G). Graph coloring is NP-hard,
and it is hard even to approximate: unless NP = ZPP, no polynomial-time
algorithm approximates χ(G) within a factor n^(1−ε) for any ε > 0.
tasks.reference: DIMACS / COLOR02 benchmark (+ gc_instances)

tasks.title: Curriculum-based timetabling
tasks.summary: Assign courses to rooms and time slots. Satisfy all hard constraints, then minimize the prescribed soft-constraint penalties.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **curriculum-based course timetabling problem (CB-CTT)**: a
university publishes curricula (sets of courses that students of a
programme take together), and every course has a teacher, a number of
weekly lectures, a minimum number of days those lectures should spread
over, and a student count. Assign every lecture to a **room** and a
**period** (day × timeslot) of the week.

A timetable is **feasible** only if it violates none of the four hard
constraints:

- **Lectures**: every lecture of every course is scheduled (no missing, no
  extra lectures);
- **Conflicts**: no two lectures share a period if they have the same
  teacher or belong to the same curriculum;
- **Availability**: no lecture sits in a period declared unavailable for
  its course;
- **RoomOccupation**: no two lectures share a room in the same period.

Among feasible timetables, quality is the **soft-constraint penalty**
(lower is better):

- **RoomCapacity**: for each lecture, 1 point per student above the room's
  seat count;
- **MinimumWorkingDays**: 5 points per day below the course's minimum
  spread;
- **CurriculumCompactness**: 2 points per lecture of a curriculum that is
  isolated (no adjacent lecture of the same curriculum on the same day);
- **RoomStability**: 1 point per additional distinct room used by a
  course.

CB-CTT is NP-hard. The instances are real university data.
tasks.reference: ITC 2007 Track 3
tasks.note: Six final instances; 240 seconds of solving time per instance.

tasks.title: Capacitated vehicle routing
tasks.summary: Route vehicles from a depot to all customers, respecting capacity and the instance’s fleet limit while minimizing total travel length.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP)**, a depot serves customers with integer demands using identical vehicles of capacity `Q`. Design routes that start and end at the depot and together visit every customer exactly once. The total demand on every route must be at most `Q`.

Where the instance specifies a fleet limit `K`, the solution may use at most `K` routes. The task checker enforces the limit encoded by the `-kK` suffix of the instance name. Among valid route collections, minimize the total travel length.
tasks.reference: CVRPLIB

tasks.title: Directed feedback vertex set
tasks.summary: A directed feedback vertex set (DFVS) of a directed graph is a set of vertices whose removal leaves the graph acyclic: delete the set, and no directed cycle survives.
tasks.question_markdown:
A **directed feedback vertex set (DFVS)** of a directed graph is a set of
vertices whose removal leaves the graph acyclic: delete the set, and no
directed cycle survives. Finding a *minimum* DFVS is NP-hard (it is one of
Karp's 21 NP-complete problems) and shows up in deadlock breaking, program
analysis, and circuit design.
tasks.reference: PACE 2022

tasks.title: Dominating set
tasks.summary: A dominating set of an undirected graph is a set of vertices D such that every vertex outside D has at least one neighbor in D.
tasks.question_markdown:
A **dominating set** of an undirected graph is a set of vertices D such
that every vertex outside D has at least one neighbor in D. The goal:
find a dominating set as **small** as possible. The decision version is
NP-complete, and getting a good approximation in polynomial time is
believed to be hard, so in practice heuristic solvers matter.
tasks.reference: PACE 2025 (heuristic track)

tasks.title: 2D guillotine glass cutting with defects
tasks.summary: Flat glass plates are cut into ordered rectangular pieces. Plates are 6000 × 3210 mm and arrive in a fixed order; each plate carries defects (small rectangles that no produced piece may overlap).
tasks.question_markdown:
Flat glass plates are cut into ordered rectangular pieces. Plates are
6000 × 3210 mm and arrive **in a fixed order**; each plate carries
**defects** (small rectangles that no produced piece may overlap).
Pieces are grouped in **stacks**, and the pieces of each stack must come
off the line **in the given sequence** (rebuilt from the cutting
patterns by a depth-first traversal). Cuts are **guillotine cuts**: a
piece must be obtainable with at most 3 cuts, plus at most one extra
"trimming" cut inside each sub-plate left after a 3-cut (a branch at cut
depth 3 or 4 has at most 2 children). First cuts are always vertical,
with widths between 100 and 3500 mm (wastes excepted); second-cut
heights are at least 100 mm; every waste rectangle is at least
20 × 20 mm. Pieces may be rotated 90°.

The **objective** is to minimize glass waste: with `m` used plates of
size `W × H`, item areas `wᵢhᵢ`, and the reusable **residual** of width
`r` on the last used plate (the full-height strip right of the last
1-cut),

```
waste = m·W·H − H·r − Σᵢ wᵢ·hᵢ          (minimize)
```
tasks.reference: ROADEF/EURO Challenge 2018

tasks.title: Balanced graph partitioning (k=4, 3% balance cap)
tasks.summary: The balanced graph partitioning problem: you are given an undirected, unweighted graph with n vertices.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **balanced graph partitioning problem**: you are given an undirected,
unweighted graph with `n` vertices. Partition the vertices into `k = 4`
blocks, minimizing the **edge cut** — the number of edges whose two
endpoints land in different blocks — subject to a **balance constraint**:
no block may hold more than `floor(1.03 * ceil(n / 4))` vertices (a 3% imbalance
tolerance). Graph partitioning is NP-hard.
tasks.reference: DIMACS10 / Walshaw partition archive (34 graphs + 9 generated)

tasks.title: Hitting set
tasks.summary: A hitting set of a set family (a hypergraph) is a set of vertices H such that every given set contains at least one vertex of H.
tasks.question_markdown:
A **hitting set** of a set family (a hypergraph) is a set of vertices H
such that every given set contains at least one vertex of H. The goal:
find a hitting set as **small** as possible. This is the hypergraph
generalization of vertex cover, and it is equivalent to set cover by
duality (swap the roles of vertices and sets). The decision version is
one of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems; parameterized by the solution
size it is W[2]-complete; and for a family of `m` sets, the greedy method gives an `H_m` approximation, where `H_m ≤ 1 + ln m`. For every fixed `ε` in `(0,1)`, obtaining a `(1−ε) ln m` approximation is NP-hard. In
practice, heuristic solvers matter.
tasks.reference: PACE 2025 (heuristic track)

tasks.title: Sports timetabling
tasks.summary: In sports timetabling you are given an even number of teams and must build a compact double round-robin schedule — every pair of teams plays twice (once at each home venue), every team plays exactly one game in every round.
tasks.question_markdown:
In **sports timetabling** you are given an even number of teams and must
build a **compact double round-robin schedule** — every pair of teams
plays twice (once at each home venue), every team plays exactly one game
in every round. On top of this backbone, the instance imposes constraints
from nine classes — capacity (CA1–CA4: how many home/away games given
teams play in given slot sets, against given opponent groups, in any
window of consecutive slots), game (GA1: how many listed games a slot set
hosts), breaks (BR1/BR2: home streaks / away streaks), fairness (FA2: differences between teams’ cumulative home-game counts at specified rounds) and
separation (SE1: minimum distance between the two legs of a pair). Some
are marked HARD in the instance; the rest are soft, and each violated soft
constraint adds its penalty to the objective. The goal: **minimize the
total soft penalty while keeping every hard constraint satisfied**. A
schedule with any hard violation is worthless (that instance scores 0).

For phased instances (`gameMode=P`), each half of the season must itself be a complete single round robin: every pair meets once in each half.

Sports timetabling is NP-hard.
tasks.reference: ITC 2021 (5th International Timetabling Competition)

tasks.title: Job-shop scheduling (makespan)
tasks.summary: In the job-shop scheduling problem (JSSP) you are given n jobs and m machines. Each job is a fixed chain of m operations; every operation occupies one specific machine for a given processing time.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **job-shop scheduling problem (JSSP)** you are given `n` jobs and
`m` machines. Each job is a fixed chain of `m` operations; every operation
occupies one specific machine for a given processing time. A machine runs
at most one operation at a time; a job's operations must run in their
given order. The goal is to minimize the **makespan** — the moment the
last operation finishes.

JSSP is one of the classical NP-hard problems of scheduling theory.
tasks.reference: JSPLib (252 classic + 31 generated)

tasks.title: Logic synthesis (minimum AIG)
tasks.summary: A completely specified Boolean function with n inputs and m outputs is given as a truth table.
tasks.question_markdown:
A completely specified Boolean function with `n` inputs and `m` outputs
is given as a **truth table**. Your job: synthesize a **combinational
circuit** that computes exactly this function, built from **two-input
AND gates and inverters** (an and-inverter graph, AIG), using **as few
AND gates as possible**. Inverters are free.

This is a practical circuit-minimization task in logic synthesis: find a small AND-inverter graph for an explicitly given truth table.
tasks.reference: IWLS 2023 Programming Contest

tasks.title: Maximum clique
tasks.summary: In the maximum clique problem you are given an undirected graph and must find the largest set of vertices that are pairwise adjacent — a clique.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **maximum clique** problem you are given an undirected graph and must
find the largest set of vertices that are pairwise adjacent — a *clique*.
The size of a largest clique is denoted ω(G). Maximum clique is NP-hard, and
it is hard even to approximate: unless NP = ZPP, no polynomial-time algorithm
approximates ω(G) within a factor n^(1−ε) for any ε > 0.
tasks.reference: DIMACS clique benchmark (classic 80-instance set)

tasks.title: Weighted maximum cut
tasks.summary: Partition a weighted graph into two sets to maximize the total weight of edges crossing the partition. The checker recomputes the objective.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **maximum cut** problem you are given an undirected graph with a
(possibly negative, possibly fractional) weight on every edge, and you must
split the vertices into two sides so that the total weight of the edges
*crossing* the split — endpoints on different sides — is as large as
possible. MaxCut is one of Karp's 21 NP-complete problems. For nonnegative edge weights, the Goemans–Williamson algorithm gives an approximately 0.87856-approximation. This benchmark also permits negative weights, beyond the assumptions of that guarantee.
tasks.reference: MQLib
tasks.note: 45 final instances; 600 seconds of solving time per instance.

tasks.title: Weighted MaxSAT
tasks.summary: In weighted MaxSAT you are given a Boolean formula in conjunctive normal form — an AND of OR-clauses over variables x1..xn — split into hard clauses, which must all be satisfied, and soft clauses, each carrying a positive integer weight.
tasks.question_markdown:
In **weighted MaxSAT** you are given a Boolean formula in conjunctive
normal form — an AND of OR-clauses over variables `x1..xn` — split into
**hard** clauses, which must all be satisfied, and **soft** clauses,
each carrying a positive integer weight. The cost of an assignment is
the sum of the weights of the soft clauses it falsifies; the task is to
find a hard-satisfying assignment of minimum cost. MaxSAT is NP-hard,
and it is the workhorse encoding for a long list of applied optimization
problems (planning, scheduling, verification, data analysis).
tasks.reference: MaxSAT Evaluation 2026 (anytime weighted set)

tasks.title: Machine reassignment
tasks.summary: Reassign processes to machines while satisfying capacity, service-conflict, location, and dependency constraints; minimize weighted load, balance, and migration costs.
tasks.question_markdown:
In the **machine reassignment problem** a set of *processes* runs on a
set of *machines*. Each process consumes an amount of several
*resources* (CPU, RAM, ...), and each machine has a finite capacity per
resource. Every process starts on an initial machine. Your job: produce
a **new assignment** of processes to machines that lowers the total cost
while respecting every hard constraint.

**Hard constraints** (all checked by the reference checker):

- **Capacity** — per machine and resource, total usage must not exceed
  capacity. *Transient usage*: a process moved away from its initial
  machine still occupies its **transient** resources on the origin
  machine (during the reassignment both machines are charged). This
  ghost usage matters for the capacity check only; the objective's
  load/balance terms below use current usage only.
- **Conflict** — two processes of the same *service* cannot share a
  machine.
- **Spread** — the processes of a service must occupy at least
  `spreadMin` distinct *locations*.
- **Dependency** — if service A depends on service B, every process of A
  must run in a *neighborhood* where at least one process of B runs.

**Objective** (weighted sum, all weights given in the model file):

- **load cost** — per machine/resource:
  `weight_r * max(0, usage - safetyCapacity)`;
- **balance cost** — per balance triple `(r1, r2, target, weight)` and
  machine: `weight * max(0, target * remaining(r1) - remaining(r2))`;
- **process move cost** — per moved process: `moveCost_p * weightPMC`;
- **service move cost** — `weightSMC * (max over services of the number
  of moved processes in that service)`;
- **machine move cost** — per moved process, a machine-to-machine cost
  from a full matrix, times `weightMMC`.
tasks.reference: ROADEF/EURO Challenge 2012
tasks.note: Ten final instances; 300 seconds of solving time per instance.

tasks.title: Nurse rostering
tasks.summary: The nurse rostering problem: you are given a planning period for one hospital ward, a set of shift types (e.g. Early/Late/Day/Night), a team of nurses each working under a contract (work regulations), a daily demand (how many nurses are needed per shift type per day), and the nurses' day-off and shift-off requests.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **nurse rostering problem**: you are given a planning period for one
hospital ward, a set of shift types (e.g. Early/Late/Day/Night), a team
of nurses each working under a contract (work regulations), a daily
demand (how many nurses are needed per shift type per day), and the
nurses' day-off and shift-off requests. Assign at most one shift per
nurse per day so that the demand is covered **exactly**, and minimize
the total penalty for broken soft constraints (contract violations such
as too many working days in a row, incomplete weekends, unwanted shift
successions, and unmet requests).
tasks.reference: INRC-I (First International Nurse Rostering Competition, 2010)

tasks.title: One-sided crossing minimization
tasks.summary: When drawing a bipartite graph in two horizontal layers, the number of edge crossings depends on the vertex order inside each layer.
tasks.question_markdown:
When drawing a **bipartite graph** in two horizontal layers, the number
of edge crossings depends on the vertex order inside each layer. In
**one-sided crossing minimization (OSCM)** the order of one layer is
fixed and you may only permute the other; the goal is an ordering with
as few crossing edge pairs as possible. The problem is NP-hard even in
this one-sided form and is the workhorse subroutine of every layered
graph drawing engine (Sugiyama-style diagrams: UML, dataflow, circuit
schematics).
tasks.reference: PACE 2024 (exact track)

tasks.title: Quadratic assignment
tasks.summary: The quadratic assignment problem (QAP): you are given n facilities and n locations, a flow matrix F (flow between facilities) and a distance matrix D (distance between locations).
tasks.question_markdown:
The **quadratic assignment problem (QAP)**: you are given `n` facilities and
`n` locations, a flow matrix `F` (flow between facilities) and a distance
matrix `D` (distance between locations). Assign each facility to a distinct
location — a permutation `p` where `p[i]` is the location of facility `i` —
minimizing the total flow-by-distance cost

```
cost(p) = sum_{i,j} F[i][j] * D[p[i]][p[j]]
```

QAP is NP-hard (it contains TSP as a special case) and, unless P = NP, no
constant-factor approximation exists (Sahni–Gonzalez 1976).
tasks.reference: QAPLIB

tasks.title: Quantified Boolean formulas
tasks.summary: Decide whether quantified Boolean formulas are true or false and supply a machine-checkable proof certificate for every answer.
tasks.question_markdown:
**QBF** (quantified Boolean formula) extends SAT with quantifiers: a
formula in prenex CNF like `∀x ∃y: (x ∨ y) ∧ (¬x ∨ ¬y)` is a two-player
game — the universal player picks `x`, the existential player answers
with `y`, and the formula is **true** if the existential player has a
winning strategy for every universal move. Deciding QBF is the canonical
PSPACE-complete problem.

Both **TRUE** and **FALSE** answers must include the task’s Q-resolution proof certificate. The checker verifies it through the `qrp2rup` and `drat-trim` chain; a correct status without a verified certificate receives no solved credit.
tasks.reference: QBFEVAL'20 (PCNF track)
tasks.note: 57 final instances; 900 seconds per instance. Certificate conversion and checking have separate limits.

tasks.title: Radiotherapy planning
tasks.summary: Match a prescribed intensity matrix exactly, attain its minimum beam-on time, and minimize the number of aperture shapes.
tasks.question_markdown:
In **intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT)** planning, an `m × n` grid specifies the nonnegative integer dose `I[i,j]` required at every cell. A multileaf collimator delivers a **shape**: a binary matrix whose exposed cells form at most one contiguous interval in each row. Different rows may use different intervals, and an empty row is allowed.

Delivering shape `S_j` for a positive integer time `b_j` adds `b_j` to every exposed cell. All shapes must have the same dimensions as `I`, and their weighted sum must equal `I` cell by cell.

This task first requires the total beam-on time to attain the structural lower bound

```
L(I) = max_i (I[i,1] + sum_{j=2}^n max(I[i,j] - I[i,j-1], 0)).
```

The judged instances admit a decomposition attaining this bound. A decomposition with total beam-on time greater than `L(I)` scores zero, even when it matches the dose exactly. Among decompositions with total beam-on time `L(I)`, the objective is to **minimize the number of shapes**.
tasks.reference: MiniZinc Challenge benchmarks

tasks.title: Set covering
tasks.summary: The set covering problem (SCP): you are given m rows and n columns. Every column j covers a fixed subset of the rows and costs an integer c_j > 0.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **set covering problem (SCP)**: you are given `m` rows and `n`
columns. Every column `j` covers a fixed subset of the rows and costs an
integer `c_j > 0`. Choose a set of columns so that every row is covered by
at least one chosen column, at minimum total cost.

SCP is NP-hard. For every fixed `ε` in `(0,1)`, approximating set cover within `(1−ε) ln m` is NP-hard, where `m` is the number of rows to cover.
tasks.reference: OR-Library (full official 87-instance set)

tasks.title: Program synthesis (SyGuS)
tasks.summary: Syntax-guided synthesis (SyGuS) is the problem of automatically writing a program: given a logical specification over unknown functions ("the output must satisfy these constraints for all inputs") and, optionally, a grammar restricting the shape of candidate programs, find a function definition that satisfies the specification.
tasks.question_markdown:
**Syntax-guided synthesis (SyGuS)** is the problem of automatically
writing a program: given a logical *specification* over unknown
functions ("the output must satisfy these constraints for all inputs")
and, optionally, a *grammar* restricting the shape of candidate
programs, find a function definition that satisfies the specification.
It is the standard formulation of program synthesis. Benchmarks in this
area span several families: conditional linear integer arithmetic
(CLIA), bit-vector programming-by-examples (PBE_BV), string
transformations from input/output examples (PBE_SLIA), invariant
synthesis (Inv), and a general family.
tasks.reference: SyGuS-Comp 2017-2019 benchmarks (deduplicated)

tasks.title: Traveling salesman (symmetric)
tasks.summary: The traveling salesman problem — given n cities and pairwise distances, find the shortest round trip visiting every city exactly once — is the emblematic NP-hard problem of combinatorial optimization.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **traveling salesman problem** — given n cities and pairwise distances,
find the shortest round trip visiting every city exactly once — is the
emblematic NP-hard problem of combinatorial optimization.
tasks.reference: TSPLIB

tasks.title: Treewidth decomposition
tasks.summary: The treewidth of a graph measures how far it is from being a tree: a tree decomposition arranges subsets of the vertices ("bags") into a tree so that (i) every edge of G lies inside at least one bag, and (ii) the bags containing any vertex v form a connected subtree.
tasks.question_markdown:
The **treewidth** of a graph measures how far it is from being a tree: a
**tree decomposition** arranges subsets of the vertices ("bags") into a
tree so that (i) every vertex of G appears in at least one bag, (ii) every edge of G lies inside at least one bag, and (iii) the bags containing any vertex v form a connected subtree. The **width**
of a decomposition is its largest bag size minus one; the treewidth of G
is the minimum width over all decompositions. Deciding treewidth is
NP-complete, and good decompositions are the workhorse of parameterized
algorithms, probabilistic inference, and compiler register allocation.
tasks.reference: PACE 2017 (heuristic track)

tasks.title: Vertex cover (exact)
tasks.summary: Return a valid vertex cover no larger than the task’s reference size on as many instances as possible.
tasks.question_markdown:
A **vertex cover** of an undirected graph is a set of vertices touching every edge: for each edge, at least one endpoint belongs to the set. Finding a smallest vertex cover is NP-hard.

tasks.title: Ryser's Conjecture
tasks.summary: The conjecture is Ryser's conjecture (attributed to Herbert Ryser, c. 1970; standard reference: DeBiasio–Kamel–McCourt–Sheats, Generalizations and strengthenings of Ryser's conjecture, Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 2021).
tasks.question_markdown:
An r-partite r-uniform hypergraph divides vertices into r parts, with each hyperedge containing one vertex from each part. A matching consists of pairwise disjoint hyperedges.

A vertex cover meets every hyperedge. Ryser’s conjecture bounds the size of a smallest such cover by r−1 times the size of a largest matching.

Current status: OpenAI has published counterexamples and Lean proofs in its [public mathematics release](https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/lean/docs/162.md). The benchmark retains the statement fixed for evaluation. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 and Kimi K3.1 Pro retrieved and adapted that public proof to the task’s fixed definitions in the evaluated runs.
tasks.reference: Ryser (c. 1970). Ryser's conjecture (tau(H) <= (r-1)*nu(H) for r-partite r-uniform hypergraphs).

tasks.title: The XOR Log-Rank Conjecture
tasks.summary: The conjecture is the XOR log-rank conjecture (Montanaro–Osborne, On the communication complexity of XOR functions, arXiv:0909.3392, 2009; parity decision tree form and best known bounds: Tsang–Wong–Xie–Zhang, Fourier sparsity, spectral norm, and the Log-rank conjecture, FOCS 2013, arXiv:1304.1245).
tasks.question_markdown:
A parity decision tree can query the XOR of any subset of input bits at each node. This is more flexible than querying a single input coordinate.

Fourier sparsity sp(f) counts the nonzero Fourier coefficients of a Boolean function. The task asks whether one universal exponent c bounds parity decision-tree depth by (1 + log₂ sp(f))^c for every Boolean function. The added 1 handles sparsity one: a nonconstant parity function has sparsity one and needs one query.
tasks.reference: Montanaro-Osborne; parity-decision-tree form Tsang-Wong-Xie-Zhang (2009/2013). XOR log-rank conjecture.
